substack_draft:note-3263012f4d06c382ed2d.text:
A bot that answers every question can make a terrible demo.

Try one question your FAQ doesn't answer. Does the bot ask for help, or invent something? That failure tells you where a person needs to take over.

The current context: OpenAI News published “How Jump Trading is scaling quant research with ChatGPT”. The following is our practice exercise, not a finding from that report.

Build a fictional shop FAQ. Test an answered question, a missing answer and conflicting details. Decide the correct behaviour first, then record the actual replies. This is a practice exercise, not a claim about a particular product.

My rule: show the awkward cases beside the successful ones. A small demo with visible limits is easier to assess than a big promise with no test results.

Which reply would make you stop trusting a bot?

Source: OpenAI News

Your coding agent is brilliant on day one and lost by day thirty. The fix isn't waiting for a smarter model; it's a harness of rules, tiered context, and durable memory files that stop the agent from forgetting its own decisions.

Source: Stack Overflow Blog

substack_draft_image_review_v1:note-238e.text:
The first session with a coding agent is crisp, but by session thirty, it starts contradicting itself.

Stack Overflow explains that agent failures are usually configuration failures, solved by building a robust harness with tiered context, a short session constitution, and durable decision logs.

• Model capability is only a fraction of what determines long-term agent success.
• Tiered context files prevent agents from blowing token budgets and forgetting module structures.
• Append-only decision logs stop agents and humans from silently reversing load-bearing architecture choices.

Without a disciplined harness, code quality decays rapidly over months of automated edits.

Create a root CONTEXT.md file for a personal project outlining your build command and invariants. Test an agent session and record whether it adheres to the instructions without re-prompting.

Source: Stack Overflow Blog
